name: White-tailed Deer
facts: A fawn is born with white spots and almost no scent, so it can hide in tall grass while its mother feeds nearby. Male deer grow a brand-new set of antlers every year and drop them each winter.

name: American Black Bear
facts: Pennsylvania's black bears are some of the biggest in the world, and a few have weighed more than 800 pounds. In winter they sleep in dens for months without eating or drinking, and cubs are born while the mother is still dozing.

name: North American River Otter
facts: Otters nearly vanished from Pennsylvania because of dirty water, but people cleaned up the rivers and released otters back in the 1980s and 90s, and now they live in rivers across the state. They can hold their breath for several minutes and love to slide down muddy banks on their bellies.

name: Indiana Bat
facts: This tiny bat weighs less than three pennies and can eat half its weight in insects in a single night. A disease called white-nose syndrome, which attacks bats while they sleep in caves all winter, has wiped out most of Pennsylvania's Indiana bats, so they need our help.

name: Northern Long-eared Bat
facts: Its long ears help it find moths hiding on leaves, which it plucks right off the plant. White-nose syndrome has killed more than nine out of every ten northern long-eared bats in Pennsylvania.

name: Allegheny Woodrat
facts: This gentle, big-eyed rat lives on rocky cliffs and collects shiny things like bottle caps and bones to store in its nest. Its numbers are falling because forests are being chopped into smaller pieces and a parasite carried by raccoons makes it sick.

name: Northern Flying Squirrel
facts: It doesn't really fly; it glides from tree to tree on a flap of skin stretched between its legs, sometimes more than 100 feet in one leap. It needs cold, old hemlock and spruce forests, and as Pennsylvania warms, those forests are shrinking.

name: Snowshoe Hare
facts: Its fur turns white every winter so it can hide in the snow, and brown again in summer. With less snow falling in Pennsylvania's winters, a white hare on brown ground is easy for predators to spot.

name: Bobcat
facts: Pennsylvania's only wild cat is about twice the size of a house cat, with tufted ears and a short 'bobbed' tail. Bobcats are so quiet and shy that most people never see one, even though they live across most of the state.

name: Fisher
facts: Fishers are one of the few animals brave enough to hunt porcupines. They disappeared from Pennsylvania over a century ago when the forests were cut down, but were brought back in the 1990s and are now spreading across the state.

name: Elk
facts: Elk once roamed all of Pennsylvania but were wiped out by the 1870s; a small herd was brought from Yellowstone starting in 1913, and today about 1,400 elk live in the mountains of north-central Pennsylvania. In fall, bull elk make a loud whistling call called a bugle that can be heard for miles.

name: Ruffed Grouse
facts: In spring the male stands on a log and beats his wings so fast it sounds like a drum starting up. Pennsylvania's state bird is disappearing from much of the state because of West Nile virus and the loss of young, brushy forests.

name: Bald Eagle
facts: In 1983 only three pairs of bald eagles nested in all of Pennsylvania, poisoned by a pesticide called DDT; after the pesticide was banned and young eagles were brought in from Canada, there are now more than 300 nests. An eagle nest can be as wide as a car and weigh a ton.

name: Peregrine Falcon
facts: The fastest animal on Earth, a peregrine can dive at more than 200 miles per hour to catch birds in midair. They vanished from Pennsylvania's cliffs in the 1960s, but now nest on bridges and skyscrapers in Pittsburgh, Harrisburg, and Philadelphia.

name: Piping Plover
facts: This sand-colored shorebird is so well camouflaged that it seems to vanish when it stands still on the beach. Piping plovers hadn't nested in Pennsylvania for over 60 years until a pair returned to Presque Isle on Lake Erie in 2017.

name: Golden-winged Warbler
facts: This little yellow-capped songbird flies all the way to Central and South America every winter and back to Pennsylvania every spring. It needs young, shrubby forests to nest in, and as those grow up into tall woods, the warbler is losing its home.

name: Cerulean Warbler
facts: The male is the color of a clear summer sky, and he sings from the very tops of the tallest trees, so he is heard far more often than seen. It is one of the fastest-declining songbirds in America, and Pennsylvania's big forests are one of its most important homes.

name: Wood Thrush
facts: Its flute-like evening song is one of the most beautiful sounds in a Pennsylvania forest, and it can actually sing two notes at once. Wood thrushes have lost more than half their numbers since the 1960s as forests shrink here and in Central America.

name: Great Blue Heron
facts: Standing four feet tall, this patient bird can freeze like a statue for minutes, then strike a fish with its spear-shaped bill faster than you can blink. Herons nest together high in trees in big groups called rookeries, sometimes dozens of nests in one spot.

name: Eastern Bluebird
facts: Bluebirds almost disappeared when the old wooden fence posts they nested in were replaced and house sparrows took over their holes. People across Pennsylvania built thousands of bluebird boxes, and the bluebirds came back.

name: Barn Owl
facts: A barn owl's heart-shaped face works like a satellite dish, catching sounds so well it can catch a mouse in total darkness. It needs old barns and open meadows to live, and as those disappear, barn owls have become rare in Pennsylvania.

name: Osprey
facts: Ospreys eat almost nothing but fish, diving feet-first into the water and carrying their catch headfirst like a torpedo. Wiped out in Pennsylvania by pesticides, they were brought back by raising chicks on platforms, and came off the state's threatened list in 2017.

name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird
facts: This bird weighs about as much as a penny, yet it flies nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, 500 miles, on its way to its winter home. Its wings beat more than 50 times every second, and it is the only hummingbird that nests in Pennsylvania.

name: Pileated Woodpecker
facts: As big as a crow with a flaming red crest, this woodpecker chisels rectangular holes into dead trees to find carpenter ants. The holes it leaves behind become homes for owls, ducks, bats, and flying squirrels.

name: Wild Turkey
facts: Wild turkeys were almost gone from Pennsylvania 100 years ago, but careful protection helped them come back to every county. They can run 25 miles per hour, fly in short bursts up to 55, and they sleep in trees at night.

name: Eastern Hellbender
facts: North America's biggest salamander can grow longer than a skateboard and breathes through the wrinkly folds of its skin. It needs cold, clean, rocky streams, so when mud and pollution wash in, hellbenders disappear; Pennsylvania students helped make it the state amphibian in 2019 to protect it.

name: Bog Turtle
facts: America's smallest turtle is only about four inches long and has a bright orange patch on each side of its neck. It lives in spring-fed, soggy meadows that are being drained and built over, so bog turtles are now among the rarest turtles in the country.

name: Eastern Box Turtle
facts: A box turtle can close its hinged shell so tightly that not even a knife blade can slip in. Box turtles can live more than 100 years, and many spend their whole life within a few acres of where they hatched.

name: Wood Turtle
facts: Wood turtles stomp on the ground with their feet to trick earthworms into coming up, then eat them. They are being lost from Pennsylvania's streams because of roads, farming, and people taking them home as pets.

name: Timber Rattlesnake
facts: Timber rattlesnakes are shy and would much rather hide than bite; the rattle is a warning that says 'please go away.' A mother gives birth to live babies and stays with them for about a week, and the snakes return to the same rocky dens every winter for their whole lives.

name: Eastern Massasauga
facts: This small, gentle rattlesnake lives in wet meadows in just a few places in western Pennsylvania. Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river-mouth,' and it is one of the rarest animals in the state.

name: Spotted Salamander
facts: On the first warm, rainy night of spring, hundreds of spotted salamanders crawl out from underground to the same pond where they were born to lay their eggs. Their eggs have tiny green algae living inside them, which give the babies oxygen.

name: Wood Frog
facts: In winter, a wood frog freezes nearly solid; its heart stops and it doesn't breathe, then it thaws out alive in spring. It wears a dark robber's mask across its eyes, and its call sounds like a quacking duck.

name: Eastern Newt
facts: A young newt is called a red eft, a bright orange creature that walks the forest floor for years before going back to the water and turning green. Its bright color warns predators that its skin is poisonous.

name: Spring Peeper
facts: This frog is smaller than a paper clip, but on a spring night a chorus of peepers can be heard more than a mile away. Each one has a dark X on its back, which is how it got its Latin name crucifer, 'cross-bearer.'

name: Brook Trout
facts: Pennsylvania's only native trout has a dark green back with worm-like squiggles and bright red spots ringed in blue. It can only live in cold, clean water, so as streams warm with the changing climate, brook trout are being squeezed into smaller and smaller spaces.

name: American Shad
facts: Shad are born in rivers, swim out to the ocean for years, and then find their way back to the very river where they hatched to lay their eggs. Dams blocked them from Pennsylvania's rivers for over a century, but fish ladders and dam removals are slowly opening the way home.

name: Lake Sturgeon
facts: A lake sturgeon is a living dinosaur with rows of bony plates instead of scales; it can grow seven feet long and live more than 100 years. It was almost fished out of Lake Erie, and today it is endangered in Pennsylvania.

name: American Eel
facts: Every American eel is born in the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda, and the tiny babies drift for a year to reach rivers like the Susquehanna. After living in fresh water for ten or twenty years, they swim all the way back to the ocean to lay their eggs.

name: Northern Riffleshell Mussel
facts: This freshwater mussel lures fish with a flap that looks like a tiny minnow, then sprays its babies onto the fish's gills to hitch a ride upstream. Nearly wiped out by pollution and dams, most of the world's remaining riffleshells live in the Allegheny River and French Creek in Pennsylvania.

name: Pennsylvania Firefly
facts: Fireflies make light inside their bodies with a chemical reaction that gives off almost no heat, more efficient than any light bulb. Each kind of firefly flashes its own secret code, and bright lights from houses and streets make it hard for them to find each other.

name: Monarch Butterfly
facts: A monarch born in Pennsylvania in late summer flies almost 3,000 miles to spend the winter in mountain forests in Mexico, a place it has never seen. Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, so planting milkweed is one of the best ways to help them.

name: Rusty Patched Bumble Bee
facts: This fuzzy bee was once common across Pennsylvania, but it has almost completely disappeared, and in 2017 it became the first bumble bee ever placed on the endangered species list. It buzz-pollinates by grabbing a flower and vibrating its wings to shake the pollen loose.

name: Regal Fritillary
facts: This big orange-and-black butterfly has vanished from nearly all of the eastern United States, and its last home east of the Mississippi is a military training ground in Pennsylvania called Fort Indiantown Gap. Its caterpillars eat only violets, so it needs open meadows full of them.

name: Luna Moth
facts: This pale green moth is as big as your hand, with long tails that spin in flight to confuse the bats that hunt it. Adults have no mouth and never eat; they live only about a week, just long enough to find a mate.

name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
facts: Pennsylvania's biggest common butterfly has yellow wings with tiger stripes, and some females are nearly all black to look like the poisonous pipevine swallowtail. Its caterpillar has two big fake eyespots that make it look like a tiny snake.

name: Eastern Hemlock
status: Pennsylvania's state tree · threatened by an invasive insect
facts: Pennsylvania's state tree can live more than 500 years, and its deep shade keeps streams cold for brook trout. A tiny insect from Asia called the hemlock woolly adelgid, which looks like bits of cotton on the needles, is killing hemlocks across the state.

name: Mountain Laurel
facts: In June, Pennsylvania's mountainsides turn pink and white when the state flower blooms. Each flower has ten tiny spring-loaded stamens that snap forward and dust visiting bees with pollen.

name: American Chestnut
facts: A hundred years ago, one out of every four trees in Pennsylvania's forests was a towering American chestnut, feeding bears, turkeys, and people with its sweet nuts. A fungus from overseas killed nearly every one, but scientists are working to breed chestnuts that can survive.

name: White Oak
facts: A single white oak can live 300 years and feed more than 500 kinds of caterpillars, plus the deer, turkeys, squirrels, and blue jays that eat its acorns. Native people and early settlers ground the acorns into flour.

name: Sugar Maple
facts: It takes about 40 gallons of sugar maple sap, boiled down, to make one gallon of maple syrup. Sap runs only when nights freeze and days thaw, so as winters warm, Pennsylvania's maple-syrup season is growing shorter.

name: Common Milkweed
facts: Milkweed is the only plant monarch caterpillars can eat, and its milky sap makes them poisonous to birds. In fall its pods split open and send hundreds of seeds floating away on silky parachutes.

name: Cardinal Flower
facts: Its flowers are the brightest red in Pennsylvania's wetlands, shaped just right for a hummingbird's beak. Most bees can't reach the nectar, so cardinal flower depends almost entirely on hummingbirds to spread its pollen.

name: Jack-in-the-Pulpit
facts: 'Jack' is the little spike standing inside a striped green hood that looks like an old-fashioned church pulpit. The same plant can be male one year and female the next, depending on how much food it has stored in its root.

name: Great White Trillium
facts: Everything about trillium comes in threes: three leaves, three petals, three sepals. Its seeds are carried off and planted by ants, and it can take seven years for a seed to become a blooming plant.

name: Swamp Pink
facts: This rare wetland flower sends up a single stalk topped with a pink pom-pom that smells faintly sweet. It grows only in a few swampy spots in Pennsylvania and nearby states, and it is protected by law.

name: Pawpaw
facts: Pawpaw is the largest fruit native to North America, and it tastes like a mix of banana and mango. Its flowers are deep maroon and smell a little like rotting meat to attract the flies and beetles that pollinate them.

name: Pink Lady's Slipper
facts: This wild orchid's pink pouch traps bees that crawl in, so they have to squeeze out past the pollen to escape. It can't grow without a special fungus in the soil, so it never survives being dug up and moved.

name: Black-eyed Susan
facts: Each 'flower' is actually hundreds of tiny flowers packed into the dark center, surrounded by golden petals. Goldfinches love its seeds, and it's one of the first wildflowers to bloom in a field after a fire or plowing.

name: Eastern White Pine
facts: The tallest tree in eastern North America, white pine can grow over 150 feet, and its needles come in bundles of five. Its straight trunks were so prized for ship masts that the king of England once claimed every big one for his navy.
